lead: Bitcoin / BTC — the Crypto Bowl recruitment drive
smaller: Gold Miners ETF / GDX — the invasion hedge with leverage
AMC Entertainment / AMC — the apes rally while Nasdaq bleeds
Affirm / AFRM — the buy-now darling loses a fifth
why_lead: The Super Bowl crypto advertising blitz is the clearest crowd-recruitment story of the weekend and is supported by pre-game, own-date previews only: CBS on crypto companies spending millions to win viewers [[n0109]], the NYT 'Crypto Bowl' preview [[n0981]], the Washington Post on a 29-year-old CEO giving away millions in bitcoin [[n0916]], Marketplace [[n0110]] and WIRED's Pets.com comparison [[n0112]], which also supplies a headline-named analog. It pairs with a concrete price setup: BTC 42,197.52 USD, +15.12% over 20 sessions but -4.35% over five, ETH -7.66%, SOL -17.92% (prior completed daily close 2022-02-13), and listed proxies COIN -5.00% and MSTR -4.74% on 11 February. Relation to strictly earlier retail notes: the 2022-02-08 lead was Bitcoin's 'crypto spring' rebound (memecoins, the FTX giveaway announcement and Al Jazeera's five-straight-days headline), 2022-02-07 carried MicroStrategy as a smaller crypto-bounce item, and 2022-02-09 ran Bitcoin as a smaller item on the Justice Department seizure. The 8 February note appeared only after this date was first drafted, so the lead was rewritten to drop the evidence those editions used (the 7 February FTX giveaway, memecoin, KPMG and 'crypto spring' headlines; the DOJ seizure, TMX futures and two-scams items) and to rest on items published 8–13 February about a new catalyst, the Super Bowl ad blitz, with the rebound now stalling rather than surging. That makes it a material update, not a carryover. Reviewer change: the CPI, big-bang-hike and central-bank-drain headlines that carried the 2022-02-11 TQQQ lead were cut back to one 10-year-yield trigger, with a US Treasury NFT money-laundering study [[n0928]] and the no-breakthrough Biden–Putin call [[n1494]] as the fresh sceptic and weekend-risk evidence. The game, its in-game ads and app traffic are after the cutoff and are not described.
why_smaller: Gold Miners ETF / GDX: the invasion-fear safe-haven trade is the day's biggest defensive move (GDX +5.67%, NOC +4.53%, gold 1,842.10 USD/oz, VIX +14.43% on 11 February) with own-date catalysts (Biden telling citizens to leave [[n1439]], embassy drawdown [[n1496]], gold safe-haven jump [[n2209]]) and the 12 February Biden–Putin call that brought a decisive-response warning and no breakthrough ([[n1487]], [[n1494]]). Relation to earlier notes: 2022-02-08 ran Exxon Mobil as a war-and-inflation hedge; this is a different instrument and mechanism (leveraged gold exposure) on evidence published 10–12 February, kept secondary.

AMC Entertainment / AMC: kept as a brief secondary carryover (160 words). Meme names rallied over five sessions (AMC +22.54%, GME +21.41%) against a falling Nasdaq while Robinhood fell 12.25%. Relation to earlier notes: the 2022-02-01 lead was GameStop and 2022-02-09 ran AMC as a smaller item on its ArcLight/URW leases and the meme tax-bill story; those citations are not reused. The 2022-02-10 note had judged the popcorn hire alone too thin, so the item rests on the completed 7–11 February move plus evidence published after the 9 February cutoff (WIRED on Robinhood [[n0785]], the NYT on activist short sellers [[n0842]], AMC's popcorn hire [[n0496]]). Reviewer change: the Financial News 'dark side' headline was dropped because it was the 2022-02-11 lead's social evidence; the break test is now the missing Robinhood engine.

Affirm / AFRM: the largest single-session drawdown on the card (-20.67% to 46.55 USD; -35.46% over 20 sessions) after results coverage (PYMNTS [[n0754]], Modern Retail [[n0755]]) plus a buy-the-dip prompt (MarketWatch [[n0861]]) and BNPL-sector doubts (Banking Day [[n0731]]); a distinct buy-the-dip-on-a-broken-darling narrative; earlier editions (2 and 3 February) mentioned Affirm only as a PayPal peer, while this item rests on its own 10–12 February results coverage.
considered_not_chosen: Peloton Interactive / PTON (+40.98% over five sessions, -7.42% on 11 February; record-low and founder pieces [[n0870]], [[n0860]]): carried as a smaller item on 7 and 8 February and as the 9 February lead; the weekend coverage is retrospective rather than a new catalyst, so not repeated.

IonQ / IONQ (+13.96% 1-session, +30.39% 5-session; Duke gate release n1836, D-Wave SPAC n1349): strong quantum lottery-ticket move, but the attention evidence is thin (quote and options-chain pages n0869, n0871), so left out in favour of four better-evidenced narratives.
ARK Innovation ETF / ARKK (WSJ 'ARK stays the course' n0882): ARKK was a 1 February smaller item; used only as a card value in the GDX item.
Semiconductor and leveraged ETF drawdowns (SOXL -14.82%, AMD -10.01%, NVDA -7.26%, TQQQ -9.42%): large moves but no distinct own-date crowd catalyst beyond the broad risk-off.
Energy and wheat (OXY +5.65%, WTI 93.10 USD/bbl, wheat +3.40%): part of the same war premium as the GDX item; not given a separate slot to keep four distinct narratives.

Avoided as possibly after cutoff: n0119 (NYT 'Crypto companies weren't the only advertising first-timers', past-tense ad review), n0120 (LA Times 'Et tu, Larry?', references the FTX Larry David spot that debuted in-game), n0970 and n0971 (ADWEEK eToro and Crypto.com Super Bowl ad pieces stamped 13 February, possibly written after airing); listed exclusions n0122, n0123, n0973, n0974, n0976–n0980, n0984, n0987, n0988 were not used.
